Uniform convergence on [-b,b] justifies expectation of the exponential series; k!>=2*3^(k-2) gives the MGF bound only for |lambda|b<3. later_canonical_mirror_delta.before: If $m=0$, then $S_m=V=0$ and the zero-variance clause holds. Suppose $m\ge1$, and fix one centered variable $Z$ with $|Z|\le b$ and let $\sigma^2=\mathbb E[Z^2]$. For every integer $k\ge2$, the power functions are Borel and $x\mapsto e^{\lambda x}$ is continuous by [F9], so their compositions with $Z$ are measurable by [F10]; the almost-sure bound gives integrability of each power. Thus $|\mathbb E[Z^k]|\le\mathbb E[|Z|^k]\le b^{k-2}\sigma^2$. For fixed real $\lambda$, the exponential series converges uniformly on $[-b,b]$: its tail is bounded by $\sum_{k>N}(|\lambda|b)^k/k!\to0$. Since $|Z|\le b$ almost surely, uniform convergence and finite linearity [F2] permit termwise expectation in [F3], and the centered first-order term vanishes.

current_manifest_row.title: Bernstein tail bound for independent bounded sums
current_manifest_row.statement: For independent centered real variables bounded by b with total variance V>0, each one-sided tail at t>0 is at most exp(-t^2/(2(V+bt/3))); if V=0 their sum vanishes almost surely.
current_manifest_row.strategy: Direct: expand the bounded-variable exponential series, bound moments by variance, factor the independent moment generating functions, optimize exponential Markov, and treat zero variance separately.
